post1.text:
Most leaders at $50M think they need better systems to scale. They actually need a harder look in the mirror.

A recent Entrepreneur piece asked whether leaders in June are still the people their January goals required. For most, the honest answer is no. Not because they stopped caring, but because leadership identity rarely keeps pace with company growth.

Here is what that means in practice for scaling companies:

1. The skills that got you to $50M are not the skills that get you to $200M. Operators have to become architects. That transition is uncomfortable and most avoid it.

2. Your team is watching how you handle pressure more than how you run meetings. Culture at scale is set by behavior under stress, not by values posters on the wall.

3. Accountability starts at the top. If your leadership team is drifting from annual goals by midyear, the problem is rarely the goals.

Scaling a company does not require a better strategy half as often as it requires a more honest leader.

What has changed about how you lead since January?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur asked a simple but uncomfortable question: are you still the leader your January goals demanded, now that it is June?

For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, this question carries real weight. At that growth stage, leadership drift does not just slow progress, it creates organizational confusion that compounds over time. Teams take their cues from the top. When a leader loses focus or consistency midyear, the whole organization feels it before anyone says it out loud.

At Autobahn, we work with leadership teams to build the kind of accountability structures that do not let this drift happen quietly. The goal is not perfection. The goal is awareness and course correction before the second half of the year becomes damage control.

Read the full article and then ask yourself the honest version of that question: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMisAFBVV95cUxNTjFYbk5hUVNZeDNsS2prdVh1X2R1NXBpM2dpdUcxcTNKclN2VmNuWTQ2RFhfT3pxVk00bnp5bVl2S1VMUDZhSm5VU1RWLVVqWW95VHVrYmRJYTdSRDB3X1NNZGI5OC1yakR5aXNFX0gtZ2tpbDFJbHhndTMySWUzcWtCSkxnbFJ2UXducXNrZVdMNjQ0TF91a0g1eVVpMmV1aXZPT25kcDRUOGNxbGNyYQ?oc=5

post3.text:
A recent Entrepreneur article asked whether leaders today are living up to the standards they set for themselves at the start of the year. It is a fair question. It is also exactly the kind of question Katherine Slain pushes leaders to sit with in Chapter 1 of our upcoming book.

Chapter 1 is called "Lead Like Lives Depend On It." Katherine does not treat leadership as a soft topic. She treats it as the single most load-bearing variable in any scaling company. The chapter surfaces something that most leadership books skip entirely: the gap between who a leader thinks they are and who their organization actually experiences.

That gap is where scaling stalls.

If you lead a company moving through serious growth, this chapter will challenge you in the right ways.

Rock Your Business, by Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: By June, most leaders have quietly lowered the bar they set in January. Not on purpose, but because scaling a company creates relentless pressure, and pressure without accountability reshapes behavior. For companies pushing from $50M toward $500M, leadership drift is not a personal failure. It is a structural problem, and it has a structural fix.

post1.text:
Most business owners think about their exit too late. By the time they're ready to sell, the decisions that determine their multiple were made years ago.

J.P. Morgan's recent breakdown of exit strategies reinforces what we see constantly at Autobahn: the owners who get the best outcomes are the ones who engineered their business for sale long before they needed to.

Here's what that actually looks like at the $50M+ level:

1. Your EBITDA margin matters less than its consistency. Buyers pay premiums for predictability, not peaks.

2. Customer concentration is a silent valuation killer. If one client represents more than 20% of revenue, expect that to show up in the offer.

3. Management dependency is priced into every deal. If you are the business, buyers discount accordingly.

The companies that achieve the highest multiples treat their exit as a strategic discipline, not a finish line event.

So here is the real question: if a buyer walked into your business today, what would they discount?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Entrepreneur makes a point that every scaling company needs to hear: waiting until you are ready to sell to build an exit plan is one of the most expensive mistakes an owner can make.

At Autobahn, we work with companies in the $50M to $500M range, and the pattern is consistent. The leaders who command strong multiples started planning three to five years out. They cleaned up their financials, reduced owner dependency, and built systems that make their business attractive to a buyer or investor on any given Tuesday.

The exit is not the end of the strategy. It is the strategy.

If you are scaling and have not mapped out what a clean exit looks like, now is the time to start. Read the full article here and then ask yourself what your business looks like from the other side of the table.

post3.text:
Forbes recently outlined the essential elements of exit planning, and the core message aligns with something Paul Belair and George Hohman tackle head-on in Chapter 2 of our upcoming book.

Chapter 2 is titled Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit, and it goes well beyond the standard advice of getting your financials in order.

What Paul and George bring to this chapter is a practitioner's lens on how buyers actually evaluate a business versus how owners think they do. Those two perspectives are often very different, and that gap costs sellers real money at the closing table.

There is one specific factor they identify that most owners overlook entirely when preparing for a transaction. It consistently moves the needle on valuation, and most advisors never bring it up.

We will be sharing more as the release gets closer.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: The best time to plan your exit was five years ago. The second best time is today. For companies between $50M and $500M, valuation multiples are not determined at the negotiating table. They are built or destroyed in the years leading up to it. Here is what the owners who walk away with the strongest deals do differently, and when they start doing it.

post1.text:
Most strategic plans fail not because of bad strategy, but because of the gap between the conference room and the front line.

Forbes recently examined why leadership teams consistently break down at the execution stage, and the findings point to something most executives already sense but rarely address directly: strategy is not a document, it is a daily operating discipline.

Here is what that means for leaders scaling past $50M:

1. Alignment is not a meeting. It is a system. If your managers cannot articulate the top three priorities without looking at a slide deck, your plan is already off the rails.

2. Accountability requires specificity. Vague goals create vague results. Every initiative needs an owner, a deadline, and a measurable outcome.

3. Execution speed is a competitive advantage. Companies that close the loop between planning and action faster than their competitors win, regardless of market conditions.

The question worth sitting with: if you removed yourself from the equation today, would your team know exactly what to do next quarter to hit your three-year target?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes breaks down exactly why leadership teams stall out when it comes to executing on strategy, and it is a pattern we see repeatedly with companies in the $50M to $500M range.

At Autobahn Consultants, we have found that the execution gap is almost never a strategy problem. It is a translation problem. Leaders craft a compelling vision at the top, and it arrives at the operational level as noise.

Scaling companies cannot afford that lag. The organizations that grow consistently are the ones that build ruthless clarity into how strategy moves from the boardroom to the floor, every single week.

If your team is strong but your results are inconsistent, this article is worth your time.

post3.text:
The conversation around strategy execution is everywhere right now, and for good reason. But most frameworks skip the part where reality hits.

In Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, titled "What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes," authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall draw on experience across wildly different industries to show how disciplined strategic planning translates into real operational traction, not just better presentations.

One thing they make clear early: the companies that scale do not just have better plans. They have better habits around how those plans get reviewed, challenged, and executed week over week.

There is a specific insight in this chapter about what separates a strategic priority from a strategic distraction that will change how you run your next planning session. We will leave the details for the book.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most leadership teams believe they have a strategy problem. They are wrong. What they have is an execution habit problem. The strategy sitting in your annual plan is only as good as what your team does with it on Tuesday morning. Here is what companies scaling from $50M to $500M have learned about closing the gap between intent and action.

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M don't have a sales strategy. They have a sales habit.

There's a difference. A habit is what your team does because it worked before. A strategy is a deliberate, repeatable system built around where revenue actually comes from and why.

Gartner recently flagged something important: AI is saving sales teams significant time, but that time is not converting into revenue. Why? Because time savings without strategic direction just means your team is doing the wrong things faster.

Here's what that means for scaling companies:

1. Activity metrics are not a proxy for pipeline health. If you can't trace each deal back to a defined motion, you don't have a strategy.

2. Who owns sales strategy at your company? If the answer is "everyone," the real answer is no one.

3. The gap between $50M and $100M is rarely a talent problem. It is almost always a structure problem.

Random acts of selling feel productive. They rarely scale.

What would change in your business if your entire team operated from one clear, written sales strategy?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Gartner made a pointed observation: AI is generating real time savings for sales teams, but Chief Sales Officers are failing to redirect that capacity toward revenue-generating activity.

This matters enormously for companies in the $50M to $500M range.

At that stage, your sales team is your growth engine. If AI hands them back five hours a week and leadership has no strategy for how those hours get deployed, you have just handed a high-performance vehicle to a driver without a map.

More capacity without more direction is not an advantage. It is a liability.

The companies that will win are the ones where sales leadership actively shapes how technology-freed time gets invested. That requires a real strategy, not a quota and a prayer.

Read the full Gartner piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiYEFVX3lxTE83YmJZYVNxUUtqV1lJanRha3hGWnFtdjJYSm5FWURzTUFrVm1uTDB2R1VRWklWVlM4cVhURDNTMVFxVmw0Ql9YZUZrdndhcC1JWFRZczVJRmxlR1REQmVvMg

post3.text:
Gartner just confirmed what Deb and Brandon lay out plainly in Chapter 4 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond.

The chapter is titled "Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation." That title is not a metaphor. It is math.

Deb and Brandon work with mid-market companies daily, and they see the same pattern. Leaders assume that because revenue is growing, a sales strategy exists. Those are not the same thing. Growth can mask absence of strategy for years, until it cannot.

One of the most valuable things this chapter surfaces is the distinction between a sales process and a sales strategy. Most companies have one. Very few have both. And the one they are missing is almost always the one that drives scale.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Your sales team is busy. Your pipeline looks active. Revenue is coming in. So why does growth feel like it keeps stalling just when momentum should be building? The hard truth is that activity is not strategy. For companies between $50M and $500M, the absence of a deliberate, written sales strategy is not a gap. It is a daily, compounding cost.

post1.text:
Your brand is not your logo. It is not your tagline. It is the feeling people get when they walk away from any interaction with your company.

JBL recently made a decision to stop organizing their marketing around campaigns and start organizing it around culture. That shift is not cosmetic. It reflects a deeper understanding that campaigns have expiration dates and culture compounds over time.

For leaders scaling past $50M, this distinction is critical. Here is what it means in practice:

First, your brand has a sensory identity whether you designed one or not. Customers are already forming impressions. The question is whether you are shaping them intentionally.

Second, consistency at scale is harder than consistency at startup. As you add channels, regions, and headcount, brand drift is the default outcome. Discipline is the only antidote.

Third, marketing that earns trust compounds. Marketing that chases attention depreciates.

At what point in your growth did you stop being intentional about what your brand actually communicates?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Marketing Dive profiles Ulta Beauty's CMO on how the brand balances long-term brand building with the demands of omnichannel marketing. It is a tension every scaling company eventually faces.

At Autobahn, we see this play out constantly with companies moving through the $50M to $500M range. The instinct is to optimize each channel independently. The result is a fragmented customer experience and a brand that means something different depending on where you find it.

Ulta's approach is a useful reminder that brand and performance marketing are not in competition. They are supposed to reinforce each other. Getting that integration right is a strategic decision, not a tactical one.

If your channels are telling different stories, your brand has a problem worth solving now. Read the full piece here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiogFBVV95cUxPRlFnSEozTXJJdnl5aWFJQTFGR0tkcnhrUnUyOTNZNlIwcHZiLWFnbm0tQ0FWZEZCTWZvdUFQeEFvQkIwOHdpMmZBR3I5WmNjRmFYb0xJMGhQWmJHYUdWUVdyWndOWTYwR1ZQQ2E4V1dMV2NrT0hpRzNaU1VKdUdoZHMwSFB4SlhYTkZKZ2hDdEdsSkJ6TW91UTZTWlNGaGVmcUE

post3.text:
JBL's move away from campaign-driven marketing toward something more cultural and sustained is exactly the kind of strategic shift that Chapter 5 of Rock Your Business addresses head-on.

The chapter is called What Does Your Marketing Smell Like? and it was written by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West. The title alone should tell you something. Marketing leaves a sensory impression whether leaders acknowledge it or not.

One of the key ideas Simpson and West explore is that growing companies often treat marketing as a series of disconnected efforts rather than a unified system with its own identity and logic. That gap becomes expensive fast.

They offer a framework for diagnosing what your brand is actually communicating versus what you intend it to communicate. The two are rarely the same.

Rock Your Business, the new book from Jonathan Slain and Katherine Slain, is available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most companies at the $50M mark have a marketing function. Very few have a brand. The difference is not budget or headcount. It is intention. When your marketing smells like something consistent, recognizable, and trustworthy across every channel and customer touchpoint, growth gets easier. When it does not, every dollar you spend on acquisition works harder than it should.

post1.text:
Hiring more people is not a growth strategy. It is a budget problem waiting to happen.

SHRM recently highlighted a shift happening across industries: companies that scaled headcount fast are now backtracking, while those that hired with precision are outperforming. The lesson is not subtle.

Here is what leaders running $50M-plus businesses need to internalize right now:

1. Every open role should be tied to a specific revenue or operational outcome. If you cannot name it, do not post the job.

2. Speed-to-hire is not a win if the person leaves in 18 months. Retention starts at the offer letter, not the 90-day review.

3. Your talent strategy should be built around where you are going, not where you have been. Hiring for today's problems creates tomorrow's misalignment.

The companies scaling from $50M to $500M are not winning because they have more people. They are winning because they have the right ones.

What is the last role you hired for that you would eliminate if you started over?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SHRM lays out what high-performing companies are doing differently in hiring right now: they are moving away from volume-based recruiting and toward precision targeting, aligning every hire to a specific business outcome before the search even begins.

For companies in the $50M to $500M growth range, this is not a nice-to-have. It is a survival skill.

At Autobahn, we see it constantly. Leaders who treat talent acquisition as a numbers game stall out. Leaders who build a talent engine anchored to their growth plan scale.

If your hiring process still looks the same as it did three years ago, it is costing you more than you realize.

Read the full SHRM piece and then ask your team: does our current hiring process actually reflect where we want to go?

post3.text:
The conversation around hiring precision is not new to us. It is central to Chapter 6 of our upcoming book.

In "Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond," Chapter 6, The Talent Engine, co-authored by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, tackles exactly why most scaling companies get people strategy wrong and what it actually takes to build a team that can carry a company through serious growth.

One thing Caleb, Darla, and Yasmin make clear: a talent engine is not an HR function. It is a core business system. And like any system, it has to be designed intentionally, not assembled by accident.

There is a specific framework in this chapter that will change how you think about your next ten hires. We will leave it there for now.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make a better business. They make a paralyzed one.

Most companies scaling past $50M fall into the same trap: they measure everything and manage nothing. A recent NetSuite breakdown of hospitality KPIs is a useful reminder that even well-intentioned metric lists can bury the decisions that actually matter.

Here is what leaders at this stage need to hear:

First, if your leadership team cannot recite your top five metrics from memory, you have too many. Complexity is not sophistication.

Second, a KPI that does not change behavior is just a number on a dashboard. Every metric you track should connect directly to a decision someone is empowered to make.

Third, lagging indicators tell you what happened. Scaling companies need more leading indicators that tell them what is about to happen.

The goal is not a comprehensive scorecard. The goal is clarity.

How many of your current KPIs have actually changed a decision in the last 90 days?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Business.com rounds up 14 tools for tracking KPIs across your business. It is a solid reference list, and worth a look if you are evaluating your current stack.

But here is the angle most scaling companies miss: the tool is rarely the problem.

When a company is pushing past $50M, the KPI breakdown is almost never about software. It is about alignment. Leaders are tracking different numbers, drawing different conclusions, and pulling in different directions without realizing it.

The right tool with the wrong metrics still produces noise. The right metrics with the wrong owner produce nothing.

Before you add another dashboard, ask whether your existing data is driving consistent decisions across your leadership team.

Read the full article here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMingFBVV95cUxQcWNPSTVTUDVYYURoVkZKa0ItNEtQbmJqWlNJTlIzUVZqclAxMHFaajNobC1JbGNkZGZVajN6MWJLT1pJcXktVG10VG8zUUljdU43NU5WR1cyNDB4QkxONlJkb3hJR2FfNzdGZHd1VWhPbTktdU1vdTEzamFWY2ZFVDNKUFIwRG91ZDdWU1UyN2twNFpLd1JjU3EzTUpjdw?oc=5

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that we named 'Death by KPIs.' That title was not an accident.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business, written by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, tackles one of the most common and costly mistakes growing companies make: confusing measurement with management.

The insight that stops most leadership teams cold is this: your KPIs may be technically correct and still completely wrong for your stage of growth. What you measured to get to $50M is not always what you need to watch to reach $500M.

The chapter gives leaders a clear way to audit their current metrics and rebuild their scorecards around decisions, not just data.

If your team spends more time updating dashboards than acting on them, this chapter was written for you.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most leadership teams think their KPI problem is a data problem. It is not. It is a decision problem. When companies scale past $50M, metric overload quietly becomes one of the biggest drags on growth. The dashboards get more sophisticated, the insight gets thinner, and nobody can agree on what actually matters. Here is how to fix that.

articles.snippet: Thousands of CEOs admit AI had no impact on employment or productivity—and it has economists resurrecting a paradox from 40 years ago  Fortune

post1.text:
Most executives are using AI wrong, and their productivity numbers prove it.

A recent Fortune analysis found that thousands of CEOs reported AI had virtually no measurable impact on employment or productivity inside their organizations. Economists are now comparing this moment to a computing paradox from the 1980s, when massive technology investment produced almost nothing on the bottom line for years.

Here is what scaling companies need to understand:

First, AI tools do not create leverage by themselves. The leader who deploys them creates the leverage. Second, companies between $50M and $500M are often adopting AI reactively, copying what larger enterprises do, without the infrastructure to absorb the change. Third, the gap between AI adopters and AI integrators is already widening. Adoption is installing a tool. Integration is redesigning how decisions get made.

The executives winning with AI are not the ones with the most tools. They are the ones who have redesigned how their teams operate around those tools.

What is your company actually doing differently because of AI, not just faster?

post2.text:
A recent piece in SmartBrief made a point worth sitting with: the companies that learn to manage AI well will win the next productivity race outright.

At Autobahn, we would take that further. For companies scaling from $50M toward $500M, AI management is not an IT conversation. It is an organizational design conversation. Who owns the outputs? How do you build accountability into AI-assisted decisions? How do you keep your best people engaged when their roles are shifting underneath them?

These are leadership questions, not technology questions. Companies that hand AI strategy to their tech team and walk away will fall behind companies where the executive team is actively shaping how AI changes the way work gets done.

If you are leading a scaling company and want a sharper lens on this, start here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMipAFBVV95cUxNTnQ4XzU3b3ZXSU12YkxxUjhOUGZxNHRqbUlwNC11dnpuaHRyQjQ0azRxVHQ0QTdHNzBXT0tVYUFDN0p0SVVWazNNMV9oVVlIbDM2MzMxNmFBXzQtWFFMVlN3S3VibWhMNGtOMFczbEtPaWE1dWRCYWNqVzQ4ck8tdXUwSFZVekZBUHBNR1Uway01WUIxLXNZMF9USmt0bG1rQjd6dQ

post3.text:
A recent New York Times piece explored how busy executives are now deploying AI versions of themselves to handle meetings, messages, and decisions they cannot get to. Fascinating concept. But it raises a harder question: if an AI can represent you, what does your team actually need from you that AI cannot provide?

Chapter 8 of Rock Your Business, titled The Third Monitor Theory and authored by Hudson Shank and Jonathan Slain, tackles exactly this tension. The chapter introduces a framework for how leaders at scaling companies can build AI into their operating rhythm without losing the human judgment that got them to $50M in the first place.

One of the core insights: the third monitor is not about watching more. It is about seeing what your business is actually telling you, in real time, so you can lead with precision instead of instinct alone.

post1.text:
The leaders most likely to derail their companies are not the incompetent ones. They are the ones who believe they do not deserve to be in the room.

Imposter syndrome does not disappear when you hit $50M in revenue. Research from Forbes Australia confirms it actually intensifies as the stakes get higher. High achievers who scaled through grit and instinct suddenly find themselves managing complexity they were never formally trained for. That gap between perceived expectation and felt capability becomes a quiet liability.

Here is what that costs scaling companies specifically:

First, leaders who feel like frauds avoid bold decisions. They wait for certainty that never comes, and competitors move faster.

Second, they over-hire to compensate, surrounding themselves with people who validate rather than challenge.

Third, they normalize their own anxiety as motivation, which eventually produces burnout at the executive level and cultural whiplash below it.

The feeling of not belonging in the role you built is not humility. It is a business risk.

How many of your best decisions were delayed because you were waiting to feel qualified enough to make them?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes Australia makes a point that should stop scaling company leaders cold: imposter syndrome does not fade as you climb. It compounds.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern constantly in companies moving from $50M toward $500M. The founder or executive who outperformed every early expectation suddenly feels unqualified to lead the organization they created. So they hedge. They avoid. They second-guess the very instincts that got them here.

For growing companies, this is not a personal struggle. It is an operational problem. Hesitation at the top filters down fast. Teams stall waiting for direction that leaders are afraid to give.

The first step is naming it accurately: this is a leadership performance issue, not a character flaw. Read the full piece and consider where this might be showing up on your leadership team.

There is a question that haunts a surprising number of leaders running eight and nine figure companies: how could I be this successful and still not feel like I belong here?

Chapter 9 of Rock Your Business, titled "How Could You Be Successful and Not Have It?", was written by Samantha Frost, Caleb Hawkins, and Rafa Loyo specifically to answer that. The chapter does not treat imposter syndrome as a mindset quirk to journal your way through. It treats it as a scaling obstacle with real consequences for team performance, decision velocity, and company culture.

One of the core insights: the very traits that drove growth to $50M are often the same ones imposter syndrome attacks first. That tension is not random, and it is not permanent if you know what you are actually dealing with.

post1.text:
The most dangerous moment in a founder's career is not the crisis. It is the exit.

Research shows that roughly three out of four founders regret selling their business within the first year. Not because the deal was bad. Because they never answered one question before the wire hit: Who am I when the company is not the answer?

Here is what leaders scaling past $50M rarely do but absolutely must:

1. Design your life before you design your exit. Know what you are moving toward, not just what you are leaving.

2. Separate your identity from your revenue number. The company is a vehicle. You are the driver. Those are not the same thing.

3. Build non-negotiables into your calendar now. Energy management at scale is a strategic decision, not a personal preference.

The operators who navigate growth without losing themselves do not stumble into balance. They engineer it deliberately, years before they need it.

So here is the question worth sitting with: If your company closed tomorrow, what would you wake up for?

#BusinessLeadership #FounderMindset #WorkLifeDesign

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune, produced in partnership with Morgan Stanley, lays out a roadmap for entrepreneurs navigating life after selling a business. It covers financial planning, identity shifts, and what comes next. Worth reading.

Here is what it does not say loudly enough: for founders scaling toward an exit, the planning has to start years earlier, not months.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. Leaders spend enormous energy engineering the transaction and almost none engineering the life that follows. By the time the deal closes, it is too late to course-correct.

If you are running a $50M to $500M company, your next chapter deserves the same rigor you apply to your P&L. Start that conversation now.

New data from Entrepreneur confirms what we hear from founders every year: most regret selling their business within twelve months. The money arrives. The clarity does not.

This is exactly what Chapter 10 of our upcoming book, Rock Your Business, addresses head-on.

The chapter is called Coming Up for Air, written by Samantha Frost alongside Jonathan and Katherine Slain. It tackles something most scaling playbooks ignore entirely: how leaders intentionally design their lives, not just their companies, as growth accelerates.

One thing Samantha makes clear in this chapter is that life planning is not a reward you earn after hitting a number. It is a practice you build into the work itself, long before any exit is on the table.

The leaders who scale without burning out have a plan for both.
